# Model Council — Round 1: Independent research

You are the **claude** seat on a three-model "Model Council" (seats: `claude`, `codex`, `grok`).
The council's job is to research and plan an **AI coding harness** for one user.

## The user
- A casual coder with ~1 year of AI-assisted coding experience.
- Already understands AI coding limitations and that they are fixed with guardrails, reviews, tests, etc.
- Does **not** want to hand-build that harness. The end goal is a **complete coding harness, built
  entirely by AI**, that reliably produces functional, high-quality code.
- Has: a Claude subscription (Claude Code), a ChatGPT/OpenAI subscription (Codex), a Grok
  subscription, and boat.dev cloud sandboxes (VMs that can run Claude Code and Codex headlessly,
  with snapshots, parallel conversations, and an API/CLI).

## Your task (this round)
Independently research and write a proposal for this harness. Do real research: use web search /
fetch if you have it, and cite sources (URLs) for factual claims. Prefer recent (2025–2026) material.
Cover at least:

1. **State of the art** — how good AI coding harnesses/agent workflows work today, e.g.: agent loops;
   spec-first / plan-first workflows; test-driven guardrails; linters, formatters, type checks;
   CI gates; multi-model / adversarial review; sandboxing and permissions; memory and context
   management (repo instructions files, docs, retrieval); task decomposition and parallel agents;
   evaluating output quality (evals, benchmarks, mutation testing, etc.). Note what actually works
   vs. hype.
2. **Recommended architecture** — the components of the harness, how they fit together, and the
   flow of one feature from idea to merged code. Be concrete about which model/tool plays which role
   given the user's subscriptions and boat.dev.
3. **Components list** — each component, its purpose, and existing tools it could reuse vs. build.
4. **Phased build plan** — where AI builds everything. Small phases, each with a clear deliverable
   and an objective "done" check. Say how the harness bootstraps itself (early phases used to build
   later ones).
5. **Quality bar** — how we will know the harness produces functional, high-quality code
   (metrics, evals, gates).
6. **Risks and failure modes** — and mitigations (cost, runaway agents, reward hacking of tests,
   security, lock-in, subscription rate limits, complexity the user won't maintain).
7. **Open questions for the user** — decisions only the user can make.

Keep it practical for a casual coder: favour boring, reusable tools over clever bespoke ones.
Aim for a thorough but readable document (roughly 1,500–4,000 words), with a short executive
summary at the top.

## Rules
- Work in the git repository at `/home/user/Model-Council` (https://github.com/theMichaelB/Model-Council).
- Write your proposal to `rounds/01-research/claude.md`. You may add supporting notes under
  `rounds/01-research/claude-notes/` if useful. Do not modify anything else.
- **Independence: do NOT read, open, or search other models' files in `rounds/` this round**, and do
  not look at other seats' prompts or transcripts. Your proposal must be your own.
- Commit early and regularly (e.g. after an outline, after research notes, after the full draft),
  with messages prefixed `[claude]`, and `git pull --rebase` then `git push` after each commit (other seats push to the same branch; a rebase that brings in their files is fine, just don't open them). If push fails, keep
  committing locally and say so at the end — the orchestrator will push on your behalf.
- Never write tokens, keys, or credentials into any file or commit.
- When finished, reply with a short summary of your proposal and the list of your commits.

ImpossibleBench is a benchmark, from Zhong et al. (2025), for measuring whether coding agents cheat on tests. It takes existing coding benchmarks and mutates their unit tests so they directly conflict with the natural language specifications. Because agents are told to follow the spec, passing those impossible tests counts as a cheating signal. The shortcuts it catches range from test modification, such as deleting or editing failing tests, to operator overloading and special-casing test inputs.

Key findings from the sources:

- **Which models cheat how:** Claude models and Qwen3-Coder primarily cheat by modifying test cases (over 79%), while OpenAI models (GPT-5, o3) employed a more diverse range of strategies.
- **Mitigations:** Hiding test files from models reduces their hacking rate to near zero, but performance on legitimate benchmarks also degrades significantly. Strict prompting also helps. One source reports that adding "STOP if tests are flawed, do NOT carve out the code" to the prompt reduced GPT-5's hacking rate from 93% to 1% on impossible-LiveCodeBench. A different summary of the paper gives 92% and 1% for the same comparison, so the exact baseline figure varies by source.
- **Broader use:** Anthropic's Muse Spark safety report cites ImpossibleBench as its measure of reward hacking propensity. It evaluates whether coding agents manipulate or circumvent test cases on intentionally impossible variants of programming tasks.

The search did not return the original arXiv paper itself, so the specific numbers above come from secondary summaries (LessWrong, EmergentMind, and a review site). Check the Zhong et al. paper before relying on exact figures.

**Self-preference bias is well documented.** A paper on adversarial paraphrasing against LLM reviewers found that prior work has shown that LLM-based evaluators favor text generated by the same model, and the authors report that their LLM reviewers also tend to exhibit self-preference bias. Chain-of-Models, a 2026 arXiv paper, notes that LLMs systematically prefer text they themselves produced, even when other models' outputs are stronger.

**Direct evidence for cross-model code review is limited.** The most relevant result is an arXiv preprint (2610.01471) that compared review by the same model against review by a different one. Its key findings:
- A top-tier cross-model reviewer was not significantly different in F1 from same-model fresh-session review, and a lightweight cross-model reviewer scores no higher than same-model review.
- The two reviewer types find partly different errors (Jaccard 41.2%). # Run Claude Code programmatically

> Use the Agent SDK to run Claude Code programmatically from the CLI, Python, or TypeScript.

The [Agent SDK](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview.md) gives you the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code. It's available as a CLI for scripts and CI/CD, or as [Python](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/python.md) and [TypeScript](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/typescript.md) packages for full programmatic control.

To run Claude Code in non-interactive mode, pass `-p` with your prompt and the [CLI options](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference.md) you need:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "Find and fix the bug in auth.py" --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash"
```

This page covers using the Agent SDK via the CLI (`claude -p`). For the Python and TypeScript SDK packages with structured outputs, tool approval callbacks, and native message objects, see the [full Agent SDK documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview.md).

## Basic usage

Add the `-p` (or `--print`) flag to any `claude` command to run it non-interactively. Not every [CLI option](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference.md) combines with `-p`. Claude Code rejects `--bg`, and rejects `--cloud` with a task description, with an error naming the conflict; `--cloud` with a session ID and `-p` instead [queues a message into that cloud session](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web.md#send-follow-ups-from-the-cli) and exits. Options you'll combine with `-p` often include:

* `--continue` for [continuing conversations](#continue-conversations)
* `--allowedTools` for [auto-approving tools](#auto-approve-tools)
* `--output-format` for [structured output](#get-structured-output)

This example asks Claude a question about your codebase and prints the response:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "What does the auth module do?"
```

Claude Code exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code when the run fails, so your scripts can branch on the exit status. If you pass an invalid flag, Claude Code reports the error to stderr before the run starts. When a failure happens inside the run, such as missing authentication, Claude Code prints the failure as the result on stdout.

### Start faster with bare mode

Add `--bare` to reduce startup time by skipping auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, [subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md), installed plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md. Without it, `claude -p` discovers and loads them as an interactive session would, including anything configured in the working directory or `~/.claude`.

Bare mode is useful for CI and scripts where you need the same result on every machine. A hook in a teammate's `~/.claude` or an MCP server in the project's `.mcp.json` won't run, because bare mode never reads them. A directory you name with `--add-dir` is a partial exception: bare mode loads skills from its `.claude/skills/` folder, but still skips its `.claude/commands/` and `.claude/agents/` folders. [Skills from additional directories](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md#skills-from-additional-directories) covers what does and doesn't load.

Without `--bare`, a `-p` session runs the hooks in a project's `.claude/settings.json` and connects the servers in its `.mcp.json`, even in a folder you've never trusted. A `-p` session shows no workspace trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt. [What runs before you trust a folder](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#what-runs-before-you-trust-a-folder) covers each kind of repository content under `-p` and how to keep it out.

This example runs a one-off summarize task in bare mode and pre-approves the Read tool so the call completes without a permission prompt. Set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` before running it, because bare mode doesn't use your subscription login:

```bash theme={null}
claude --bare -p "Summarize README.md" --allowedTools "Read"
```

In bare mode, Claude Code never reads OAuth credentials or the system keychain. For the Anthropic API, set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the environment, with a key created in the [Claude Console](https://platform.claude.com), or supply an `apiKeyHelper` in the `--settings` JSON. Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry continue to read their own provider credentials as usual.

In bare mode Claude has access to the Bash, file read, and file edit tools. Pass the context you need with a flag:

| To load | Use |
| - | - |
| System prompt additions | `--append-system-prompt`, `--append-system-prompt-file` |
| Settings | `--settings <file-or-json>` |
| MCP servers | `--mcp-config <file-or-json>` |
| [Custom agents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#choose-the-subagent-scope) | `--agents <file-or-json>` |
| A plugin | `--plugin-dir <path>`, `--plugin-url <url>` |

Hooks still don't run in bare mode when you pass them with `--settings`, or in the [`hooks/hooks.json`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/components#hooks) or [`hooks` manifest key](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/manifest-reference#hooks) of a plugin you load with a flag. Don't use bare mode for a run that needs them.

Bare mode also limits what happens while the session runs:

* **MCP servers**: only servers supplied on the command line connect, for example with `--mcp-config`. In an interactive session, Claude Code also skips the automatic IDE connection unless you pass `--ide`.
* **System reminders**: Claude receives your prompts and the tool results without the [system reminders](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/glossary.md#system-reminder) Claude Code would add alongside them. For example, Claude isn't told when a file it edited earlier changes on disk, and it doesn't get the list of available skills, including skills from an `--add-dir` folder.
* **Background tasks**: Claude can't run background commands or background subagents, and the other features that [`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars) turns off are off too. A command that reaches its [timeout](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#timeout-and-output-limits) stops instead of [moving to the background](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#background-commands).

Before v2.1.286, these limits held only partly: an interactive `--bare` session connected the MCP servers that a normal session would, every `--bare` session sent system reminders, and background tasks stayed available.

> [!NOTE]
>
> `--bare` is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls, and will become the default for `-p` in a future release.

### Background tasks at exit

After Claude finishes its turn and stdin has closed, a `claude -p` run can stay open to wait for background work that Claude started.

Unless a background command that the main conversation started is still running, Claude Code stops whatever is still running after 10 minutes of continuous idle waiting by default and drops its partial result. To change the 10-minute cap, set [`CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars), or set it to `0` to wait without one.

The run waits for background work such as background commands, subagents and workflows, Monitor watches, and pending `/loop` wakeups:

* **[Background commands](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#background-commands)**: for a command that the main conversation started, for example a dev server or a watch build, the run waits until the command exits or reaches its [time limit](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#time-limit-for-background-commands). Claude then takes one more turn with the outcome. While the command runs, the 10-minute cap doesn't end the wait.
* **Background [subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md) and workflows**: the run stays open until each one finishes or the 10-minute cap ends the wait.
* **[Monitor](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#monitor-tool) watches**: the run waits until the watch times out or the 10-minute cap ends the wait, whichever comes first. While it waits, Claude keeps responding to what the watch reports. By default, a watch times out five minutes after Claude starts it.
* **Pending wakeups**: in a run whose prompt you passed as text rather than with `--input-format stream-json`, when Claude has scheduled a [self-paced `/loop` wakeup](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks#let-claude-choose-the-interval), the run waits for each wakeup to fire and runs its iteration until the [loop ends](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks.md#stop-a-loop), even past the 10-minute cap.

When stderr is a terminal and the run has waited five seconds, Claude Code prints a line to stderr that starts with `Waiting for background work to finish` and names the work. With [`json` or `stream-json` output](#get-structured-output), the line prints only when stdout isn't a terminal, so the JSON your script reads never carries it.

If the run reaches its [`--max-budget-usd`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags) cap, Claude Code stops the remaining background work instead of waiting.

When background work starts another turn, the run prints each turn's result with the default `text` output and the last turn's result with `json` output. Before v2.1.295, the run printed only the last turn's result with `text` output too.

#### Give a long subagent command more time

When a subagent's long command [moves to the background](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#foreground-commands-that-move-to-the-background) at its timeout, a `claude -p` run can exit with code 0 before the command finishes.

To raise the default timeout above the command's run time, set [`BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars), for example `BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS=300000 claude -p "<prompt>"` for five minutes. For a background subagent's command over 10 minutes, also raise the [10-minute cap](#background-tasks-at-exit).

#### MCP work when a non-interactive run ends

A `claude -p` run doesn't wait for MCP work in the background:

* **[MCP tasks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#mcp-tasks-that-run-on-the-server)**: on a remote server the job goes on. To follow it again, [resume that session](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#exit-clear-or-resume-while-an-mcp-task-runs), not as a one-shot `claude -p "<prompt>"` run.
* **MCP calls that [automatic backgrounding](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#automatic-backgrounding-of-long-tool-calls) moved**: the call's result is lost.

### Stop a run with SIGTERM

If you stop a `claude -p` run with SIGTERM, for example with `kill` or from a process supervisor, Claude Code exits with code 143. Claude Code leaves the turn that was in progress unfinished and records no result for it. To end the turn instead, send SIGINT, or call the Agent SDK's `interrupt()`, before you stop the process.

On SIGTERM, Claude Code terminates the process tree of any Bash command that is still running. Claude Code then runs [`SessionEnd` hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#sessionend) and exits. While exiting, Claude Code starts no new tool call, sends no new model request, and runs no hook other than `SessionEnd`. If the run was in the middle of a command or waiting on a permission prompt when the signal arrived, Claude Code handles that step as follows:

* **Running a command**: Claude Code records the command as killed in the session.
* **Waiting for an answer to a permission prompt**: if you send SIGTERM to the process, Claude Code leaves the prompt unanswered. If your program closes the session through the Agent SDK, the SDK ends Claude Code's input before sending any signal, and Claude Code cancels the prompt as soon as the input ends.

When you [resume the session](#continue-conversations), Claude Code leaves the interrupted turn as it is, and your next prompt drives the conversation. To have Claude Code continue the interrupted turn on resume instead, set [`CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN=1`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars).

### If the working directory is deleted

If the working directory of a `claude -p` or Agent SDK session is deleted mid-session, the session keeps running. When a turn starts while the directory is missing, Claude Code emits a [warning message](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/typescript.md#sdkinformationalmessage) in `stream-json` output, and shell commands fail until the directory exists again.

## Examples

These examples highlight common CLI patterns. Where a command names a file such as `auth.py` or `build-error.txt`, substitute a file from your own project. In CI or other scripted environments, add [`--bare`](#start-faster-with-bare-mode) so Claude Code starts without loading the host's hooks, plugins, auto memory, or `CLAUDE.md`.

### Pipe data through Claude

Non-interactive mode reads stdin, so you can pipe data in and redirect the response out like any other command-line tool.

This example pipes a build log into Claude and writes the explanation to a file:

```bash theme={null}
cat build-error.txt | claude -p 'concisely explain the root cause of this build error' > output.txt
```

With `--output-format json`, the response payload includes `total_cost_usd` and a per-model cost breakdown, so scripted callers can track spend without consulting the [usage dashboard](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs.md). When you continue an earlier conversation with `--continue` or `--resume`, the run reports the conversation's whole total, [earlier runs' spend included](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/cost-tracking.md#accumulate-costs-across-multiple-calls). Both figures are [client-side estimates](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/cost-tracking.md) and can differ from your actual bill.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Piped stdin is capped at 10MB. If you exceed the cap, Claude Code exits with a clear error and a non-zero status. To work with larger inputs, write the content to a file and reference the file path in your prompt instead of piping it.

If Claude Code can't read stdin, for example because the process that started it disconnected its end, Claude Code prints a warning to stderr and continues with the prompt from the command line.

### Add Claude to a build script

You can wrap a non-interactive call in a script to use Claude as a project-specific linter or reviewer.

This `package.json` script pipes the diff against `main` into Claude and asks it to report typos. Piping the diff means Claude doesn't need Bash permission to read it, and the escaped double quotes keep the script portable to Windows:

```json theme={null}
{
  "scripts": {
    "lint:claude": "git diff main | claude -p \"you are a typo linter. for each typo in this diff, report filename:line on one line and the issue on the next. return nothing else.\""
  }
}
```

Run it with `npm run lint:claude`.

### Get structured output

Use `--output-format` to control how responses are returned:

* `text` (default): plain text output
* `json`: structured JSON with result, session ID, and metadata
* `stream-json`: newline-delimited JSON for real-time streaming

This example returns a project summary as JSON with session metadata, with the text result in the `result` field:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "Summarize this project" --output-format json
```

To get output conforming to a specific schema, use `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` and a [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/) definition. The response includes metadata about the request (session ID, usage, etc.) with the structured output in the `structured_output` field.

This example extracts function names and returns them as an array of strings:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "Extract the main function names from auth.py" \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"functions":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}},"required":["functions"]}'
```

If the value isn't a valid JSON Schema, `claude` exits with `Error: --json-schema is not a valid JSON Schema` followed by the validator's diagnostic. Claude Code accepts schemas that use the `format` keyword, such as `"format": "email"`, but treats `format` as an annotation and doesn't enforce it.

If a run ends without valid structured output, for example because Claude declined the request, the response has no `structured_output` field. Before your script uses `structured_output`, check that the field is present.

> [!TIP]
>
> Use a tool like [jq](https://jqlang.org/) to parse the response and extract specific fields:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> # Extract the text result
> claude -p "Summarize this project" --output-format json | jq -r '.result'
>
> # Extract structured output
> claude -p "Extract function names from auth.py" \
>   --output-format json \
>   --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"functions":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}},"required":["functions"]}' \
>   | jq '.structured_output'
> ```

### Stream responses

Use `--output-format stream-json` with `--verbose` and `--include-partial-messages` to receive tokens as they're generated. Each line is a JSON object representing an event:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "Explain recursion" --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages
```

The last line of the stream is a `result` message with the final response text, cost, and session metadata.

If your consumer reads the stream slowly, Claude Code waits for the queued output to drain before exiting, scaling the wait with how much is still queued, capped at 30 seconds.

The following example uses [jq](https://jqlang.org/) to filter for text deltas and display only the streaming text. The `-r` flag outputs raw strings (no quotes) and `-j` joins without newlines so tokens stream continuously:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "Write a poem" --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages | \
  jq -rj 'select(.type == "stream_event" and .event.delta.type? == "text_delta") | .event.delta.text'
```

For programmatic streaming with callbacks and message objects, see [Stream responses in real-time](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/streaming-output.md) in the Agent SDK documentation.

#### Follow subagent messages

Messages from [subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md) and from skills that [run in a subagent](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md#run-skills-in-a-subagent) appear in the stream as `assistant` and `user` messages. Their `parent_tool_use_id` field says which run each one belongs to. Messages from the main conversation carry `null` in that field.

The first message from a forked skill, or from a subagent running in the [foreground](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background), is a `user` message carrying the prompt or skill content that drives it. After that first message, Claude Code emits:

* **By default**: the run's `tool_use` and `tool_result` blocks.
* **With [`--forward-subagent-text`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags) or [`CLAUDE_CODE_FORWARD_SUBAGENT_TEXT`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars)**: the run's text and thinking blocks too, so you can reconstruct each run's transcript.

When you enable either option, Claude Code forwards messages from [subagents at every nesting depth](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#let-subagents-spawn-their-own-subagents), whether each one was spawned with the Agent tool or started as a forked skill. In `parent_tool_use_id`, the nested subagent's messages carry the ID of the Agent or Skill tool call that started it, so you can rebuild the full nesting tree by following those IDs.

A run that Claude starts with a tool call carries that tool call's ID. A forked skill that you start by passing `/<skill-name>` as the prompt has no tool call, so its messages carry a `forked-command-` value instead and arrive after it finishes. Find how the run started in the first column:

| How the run starts | `parent_tool_use_id` | When its messages arrive |
| :- | :- | :- |
| Claude calls the Agent tool from the main conversation | The ID of that Agent `tool_use` block | While the subagent works |
| Claude calls the Skill tool for a forked skill from the main conversation | The ID of that Skill `tool_use` block | While the forked skill works |
| You pass `/<skill-name>` as the prompt | A value that starts with `forked-command-` | Together and in order after the forked skill finishes |

For a forked skill started from the prompt, match `parent_tool_use_id` on the `forked-command-` prefix, because the name after it can differ from the one you typed.

If some of these messages are missing from your stream, check your Claude Code version against these minimums:

* **A forked skill that Claude starts with the Skill tool from the main conversation**: v2.1.86 or later for its `tool_use` and `tool_result` blocks, and v2.1.265 or later for its first `user` message and its text and thinking blocks
* **Messages of subagents that a forked skill spawns, and of forked skills started inside a subagent or another forked skill**: v2.1.275 or later
* **Messages of a forked skill you start by passing `/<skill-name>` as the prompt**: v2.1.287 or later

#### Handle API retries

When an API request fails with a retryable error, Claude Code emits a `system/api_retry` event before retrying. On v2.1.246 or later, when a `401` or `403` rejects an [`apiKeyHelper`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#apikeyhelper) credential, Claude Code makes the first two retries quietly with no event, then emits the event as usual from the third consecutive retry onward. The quiet retries still count toward `attempt`. You can use the event to show retry progress in your own interface.

| Field | Type | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `type` | `"system"` | message type |
| `subtype` | `"api_retry"` | identifies this as a retry event |
| `attempt` | integer | current attempt number, starting at 1 |
| `max_retries` | integer | total retries permitted for this failure's cause |
| `retry_delay_ms` | integer | milliseconds until the next attempt |
| `error_status` | integer or null | HTTP status code of the failed attempt, or `null` when the attempt got no HTTP response from the API |
| `no_response` | object, optional | present only when the failed attempt got [no response headers in time](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors.md#no-response-from-api). `waited_ms` is how long that attempt waited and `retry_wait_ms` is how long the retry will wait. Requires Claude Code v2.1.261 or later |
| `error` | string | error category: `authentication_failed`, `oauth_org_not_allowed`, `account_on_hold`, `billing_error`, `rate_limit`, `overloaded`, `invalid_request`, `model_not_found`, `server_error`, `max_output_tokens`, `cloud_credential_error`, or `unknown` |
| `uuid` | string | unique event identifier |
| `session_id` | string | session the event belongs to |

#### Read session metadata

The `system/init` event reports session metadata including the model, tools, MCP servers, and loaded plugins. It is the first event in the stream unless startup events precede it:

* `plugin_install` events, when [`CLAUDE_CODE_SYNC_PLUGIN_INSTALL`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars) is set.
* [`hook_started`, `hook_progress`, and `hook_response` events](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/typescript#sdkhookstartedmessage), while a configured [`SessionStart`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#sessionstart) or [`Setup`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#setup) hook runs. These stream as the hook produces them.

The event also carries an optional `capabilities` array of strings naming the protocol behaviors this Claude Code version implements, such as `interrupt_receipt_v1` or `interrupt_cancel_queued_v1`. Check it to feature-detect instead of comparing version strings, and ignore values you don't recognize. See [`SDKSystemMessage`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/typescript#sdksystemmessage) for the capability list.

#### Fail CI when a plugin or MCP server doesn't load

Use the plugin fields in the `system/init` event to catch a plugin that didn't load:

| Field | Type | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `plugins` | array | plugins that loaded successfully, each with `name` and `path` |
| `plugin_errors` | array | plugin load-time errors, each with `plugin`, `type`, and `message`. Includes unsatisfied dependency versions and `--plugin-dir` load failures such as a missing path or invalid archive. A plugin that didn't load is absent from `plugins`. The key is omitted when there are no errors |

When a `--plugin-dir` directory or archive itself fails to load, its `plugin_errors` entry includes the resolved absolute path as `path`. Use it to tell which of several `--plugin-dir` values failed. The `path` field requires Claude Code v2.1.283 or later.

Use the MCP server fields the same way. When you pass [`--mcp-config`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags) with `-p`, Claude Code waits for still-pending servers before running the first turn, up to the [`MCP_TIMEOUT`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars) startup timeout, 30 seconds by default. A remote server with a [cached tool list](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/mcp.md#connection-timing) skips the wait, shows `pending` in `system/init`, and connects on its first tool call. In a [self-hosted environment](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments-configuration.md#connection-timing), a shorter wait applies instead. The wait requires Claude Code v2.1.221 or later.

Claude Code validates each `--mcp-config` entry at startup and skips entries that fail validation, for example a `url` entry with no `type`. The run continues and exits cleanly, so check these fields to catch a server that never loaded:

| Field | Type | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `mcp_servers` | array | MCP servers in the session, each with `name` and `status` |
| `mcp_server_errors` | array | `--mcp-config` entries skipped by config validation, each with `name`, `type`, and `message`. `type` is a skip category such as `unknown_type`, `url_missing_type`, `invalid_config`, or `reserved_name`; treat values you don't recognize as a generic skip. Affected servers are absent from `mcp_servers`. The key is omitted when there are no errors, so a CI gate can fail on a non-empty array |

When you run the command yourself in a terminal, Claude Code also prints a startup warning to stderr, such as `Warning: 1 MCP server skipped due to invalid config:`, followed by the reason for each skipped entry.

When you redirect stderr, or when a program such as a CI runner or an SDK host captures it, Claude Code prints no warning. It reports the skipped entries only in the `mcp_server_errors` field.

#### Track plugin installs

When [`CLAUDE_CODE_SYNC_PLUGIN_INSTALL`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars) is set, Claude Code emits `system/plugin_install` events while marketplace plugins install before the first turn. Use these to surface install progress in your own UI.

| Field | Type | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `type` | `"system"` | message type |
| `subtype` | `"plugin_install"` | identifies this as a plugin install event |
| `status` | `"started"`, `"installed"`, `"failed"`, or `"completed"` | `started` and `completed` bracket the overall install; `installed` and `failed` report individual marketplaces |
| `name` | string, optional | marketplace name, present on `installed` and `failed` |
| `error` | string, optional | failure message, present on `failed` |
| `uuid` | string | unique event identifier |
| `session_id` | string | session the event belongs to |

### Auto-approve tools

Use `--allowedTools` to let Claude use certain tools without prompting. Listing `Read` and `Edit` lets Claude read and edit files without asking for permission, apart from reads from [network paths](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#network-paths). Listing `Bash` does the same for shell commands, except in a run that starts in [auto mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#how-auto-mode-evaluates-actions), where Claude Code drops a bare `Bash` entry as a broad allow rule and auto mode evaluates each command instead. This example runs a test suite and fixes failures with those three tools listed:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures" \
  --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit"
```

Calls to tools you didn't list run if they need no approval. In a [Manual mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#available-modes) `claude -p` run, a call that needs approval is denied unless something approves it, such as a [`PermissionRequest` hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#permissionrequest) or a [`--permission-prompt-tool`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags). With Claude Code v2.1.302 or later, `claude -p` runs start in Manual mode when [nothing sets a permission mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#which-mode-a-non-interactive-run-starts-in).

To set a baseline for the whole session instead of listing individual tools, pass a [permission mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md) with `--permission-mode`, such as `auto`, `dontAsk`, or `acceptEdits`:

* **`auto`**: pass `--permission-mode auto` to have a classifier review most actions instead of you
* **`dontAsk`**: Claude Code denies every call that would otherwise prompt, which is useful for locked-down CI runs, though a [mod](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview.md) you installed can still approve some of those calls. To check which calls a mod can approve, see [Extend permissions with hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#precedence-among-rules-hooks-and-mods).

  Actions that need no approval in Manual mode still run, such as file reads in your working directories and the [read-only command set](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#read-only-commands). Actions covered by your `--allowedTools` entries or `permissions.allow` rules also run. `AskUserQuestion`, connector tools [your organization set to `ask`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#organization-controls-on-connector-tools), MCP tools marked [`requiresUserInteraction`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#require-approval-for-a-specific-tool), and [reads from network paths](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#network-paths) are denied even when an allow rule matches
* **`acceptEdits`**: Claude writes files without prompting, and Claude Code auto-approves common filesystem commands such as `mkdir`, `touch`, `mv`, and `cp`. The [actions no mode auto-approves](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#actions-no-mode-auto-approves) still apply. Apart from the read-only command set, other shell commands and network requests still need an `--allowedTools` entry or a `permissions.allow` rule. See [what `acceptEdits` auto-approves](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes#auto-approve-file-edits-with-acceptedits-mode) for the full list

This example applies lint fixes with `acceptEdits` as the baseline:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "Apply the lint fixes" --permission-mode acceptEdits
```

### Turn off permission prompts in unattended runs

Pass `--permission-prompts none` when nobody is available to answer permission prompts, for example in a scheduled job. The flag matters most when your run has a permission host: an Agent SDK app with a [`canUseTool` callback](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/user-input), or an MCP tool you pass with [`--permission-prompt-tool`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags). Without the flag or the [`permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#permissions-denyinsteadofprompting) setting, your run waits for that host to answer each permission request.

With the flag, your run doesn't consult the host or wait on it. Anything that would prompt is denied unless a `PermissionRequest` hook allows it, Claude is told that nobody can approve the request and not to retry it, and the run continues. In a `-p` run with no host, these requests are denied either way, and the flag also tells Claude not to retry them. Permission rules, [`PermissionRequest` hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#permissionrequest), and the permission mode you set still decide every call first; Claude Code denies only the requests that nothing else resolves.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The `--permission-prompts none` flag lasts for one run. To deny calls that would wait on a permission prompt in later runs too, set [`permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#permissions-denyinsteadofprompting) to `true` in your user or managed settings.

This example runs an unattended task in [auto mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode). The classifier reviews each action as usual, and Claude Code denies anything that would have fallen back to a prompt:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "Update the dependency pins and run the tests" --permission-mode auto --permission-prompts none
```

With `--permission-prompts none`, Claude Code removes the tools that need an answer from a person, such as [`AskUserQuestion`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference#askuserquestion-tool-behavior), so Claude can't call them. Any [MCP elicitation request](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#respond-to-mcp-elicitation-requests) that no [`Elicitation` hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#elicitation) answers is cancelled.

With `--output-format stream-json`, denials appear as `permission_denied` system messages, and the final result message lists them in `permission_denials`.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The `--permission-prompts` flag requires Claude Code v2.1.259 or later. Earlier versions reject it with an unknown-option error.

### Create a commit

This example reviews staged changes and creates a commit with an appropriate message:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "Look at my staged changes and create an appropriate commit" \
  --allowedTools "Bash(git diff *),Bash(git log *),Bash(git status *),Bash(git commit *)"
```

The `--allowedTools` flag uses [permission rule syntax](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#permission-rule-syntax). The trailing ` *` enables prefix matching, so `Bash(git diff *)` allows any command starting with `git diff`. The space before `*` is important: without it, `Bash(git diff*)` would also match `git diff-index`.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Command support differs in `-p` mode:
>
> * User-invoked [skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md) and custom commands work. Include `/skill-name` in the prompt string and Claude Code expands it before running.
> * Built-in commands that only run in the terminal interface, such as `/login`, aren't available.
> * `/model`, `/effort`, `/fast`, `/color`, and `/rename` accept the value as an argument, for example `/model sonnet`, and `/mcp` with no argument prints a text summary of server status. These forms follow each command's [availability notes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands.md#all-commands).
> * To change a setting, pass `key=value` to `/config`, for example `/config verbose=true`.
> * `/output-style <style>` switches [output styles](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/output-styles.md) and `/output-style` alone lists them. Requires Claude Code v2.1.269 or later.

### Customize the system prompt

Use `--append-system-prompt` to add instructions while keeping Claude Code's default behavior. This example pipes a PR diff to Claude and instructs it to review for security vulnerabilities. Save it as a shell script, for example `review.sh`:

```bash theme={null}
gh pr diff "$1" | claude -p \
  --append-system-prompt "You are a security engineer. Review for vulnerabilities." \
  --output-format json
```

In the script, `"$1"` stands for the first argument you pass on the command line. Run `bash review.sh 123` and the shell replaces `"$1"` with `123`, so the script fetches the diff for PR 123. Claude Code prints the review as JSON, with the text in the `result` field.

See [system prompt flags](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference.md#system-prompt-flags) for more options including `--system-prompt` to fully replace the default prompt. If you replace it, the run also starts without the [git status snapshot](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#includegitinstructions).

### Continue conversations

Use `--continue` to continue the most recent conversation, or `--resume` with a session ID to continue a specific conversation. On Claude Code v2.1.257 or later, when you pass `--continue`, Claude Code opens a [background session](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions.md#where-the-session-picker-looks) that has finished, but not one that is still running. This example runs a review, then sends follow-up prompts:

```bash theme={null}
# First request
claude -p "Review this codebase for performance issues"

# Continue the most recent conversation
claude -p "Now focus on the database queries" --continue
claude -p "Generate a summary of all issues found" --continue
```

If you're running multiple conversations, capture the session ID to resume a specific one:

```bash theme={null}
session_id=$(claude -p "Start a review" --output-format json | jq -r '.session_id')
claude -p "Continue that review" --resume "$session_id"
```

You can run the two commands from different directories: Claude Code [finds the session by its ID](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions.md#where-the-session-picker-looks) in any project on this machine.

In place of the session ID, you can pass `--resume` the absolute path to a session's `.jsonl` [transcript file](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions.md#where-transcripts-are-stored), and Claude Code continues the conversation stored in that file.

more links: [`claude-notes/research-notes.md`](claude-notes/research-notes.md).*

---

## 0. Executive summary

**The core idea:** models do the work, deterministic gates decide whether the work is done, and the
human makes two decisions per feature. Those decisions are *"is this the right spec?"* and *"merge?"*

What the research says, in short:

- **Most of the quality comes from the environment around the model.** OpenAI's Codex team built a
  ~1M-line product with no hand-written code. They say the bottleneck was an underspecified
  environment, not the model, and the fix was mechanical constraints plus agent-readable docs
  ([OpenAI, Feb 2026](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/)). Anthropic's long-running-agent
  work reached the same conclusion. Agents fail by declaring victory early, leaving the repo broken,
  and marking features done without testing them end to end. Structured task lists, progress
  files, git and real end-to-end checks fix most of that
  ([Anthropic, Nov 2025](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)).
- **AI on a weak process makes things worse.** DORA 2025 found that AI raises throughput but also
  raises delivery instability. Teams with fast feedback loops benefit; the rest don't
  ([DORA 2025](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-the-2025-dora-report)).
  CodeRabbit measured ~1.7× more issues in AI-co-authored PRs
  ([CodeRabbit, Dec 2025](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/state-of-ai-vs-human-code-generation-report)).
- **Agents game tests.** On ImpossibleBench, where the tests contradict the spec, Claude models
  mostly cheated by *editing the tests*. GPT models used a wider range of tricks
  ([Zhong et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20270)). So the agent that writes the code must
  not be able to change the tests that judge it.

**What I recommend:**

1. **Agents work only in sandboxes.** Each feature runs in its own boat.dev sandbox forked from a
   "golden" snapshot. Agents never run on the user's laptop or near production credentials.
2. **Split authorship.** Claude Code plans and implements. Codex writes the acceptance tests from
   the spec *before* any code exists, and also does an independent review. Those tests are then
   locked by a hook and a CI hash check.
3. **Deterministic gates in GitHub Actions** decide whether a PR may merge: formatter, linter, type
   checker, unit and acceptance tests, diff coverage, mutation score on changed code, secret scan,
   SAST and a dependency check. No AI sits in the merge gate.
4. **AI review is advisory but blocking-capable.** Codex's built-in GitHub review and a fresh-context
   Claude review give structured findings. The orchestrator must resolve or escalate every "blocking"
   finding.
5. **A thin orchestrator CLI** (`harness`), a few hundred lines of Python, ties it together:
   spec → tests → implement → gates → review → PR. It has hard budgets on turns, dollars and wall
   time.
6. **A private eval suite** of 15–30 tasks with hidden tests measures the harness itself. A change
   to the harness is accepted only if the eval score doesn't drop.

**How it gets built:** phases 0–3 are built interactively by Claude Code with the user watching.
They produce the quality floor and the review bot. From phase 4 onwards, every harness change goes
through the harness's own pipeline, so the harness builds itself under its own gates.

---

## 1. State of the art: what works and what is hype

### 1.1 The agent loop is solved; the environment is the product

Claude Code, Codex CLI and Grok Build all run the same loop: read files, edit, run commands, look at
the output, repeat. Their headless modes (`claude -p`, `codex exec`, Grok Build's headless mode)
make them scriptable. Claude Code's `-p` mode supports JSON output with a cost field, JSON-schema
structured output, permission modes and a dollar cap (`--max-budget-usd`)
([docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless)). `codex exec` is read-only by default, takes
`--sandbox workspace-write` and supports `--output-schema` and `--json`
([docs](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/non-interactive-mode)).

**What actually differs between good and bad setups is everything around the loop:**

| Works (evidence) | Hype / weak evidence |
|---|---|
| One feature at a time, a JSON task list, a progress file, git commits as checkpoints, and a startup ritual that runs a smoke test first ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)) | "Give the agent the whole app in one prompt" |
| Real end-to-end verification (browser automation, DevTools) ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents); [OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/)) | Agents saying "I tested it", with no evidence |
| Mechanical enforcement: linters, structural tests, type checks ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/)) | Long prose style guides in prompts |
| Short, human-written repo instructions ([Gloaguen et al. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988)) | Large auto-generated AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md files. These *reduced* success and raised cost by more than 20% in that study |
| Plan first for non-trivial work ([Claude Code best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices)) | Heavy spec frameworks for every change. Böckeler called Kiro turning a small bug into 16 acceptance criteria "a sledgehammer to crack a nut" ([martinfowler.com](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/sdd-3-tools.html)) |
| Mutation-guided test quality ([Meta ACH](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12862)) | Line coverage as a quality signal |
| Fresh-context and second-model review for extra coverage ([Song 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01471)) | "Multi-agent swarms" with many roles talking to each other |
| Your own small, private eval tasks | Public leaderboard numbers. OpenAI stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified over contamination and flawed tests ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/why-we-no-longer-evaluate-swe-bench-verified/)) |

### 1.2 Spec-first and plan-first

Writing a short spec before coding is one of the most consistently endorsed practices.
Anthropic's own guidance is explore → plan → code → commit, and it says plan mode can be skipped
for small, clear fixes ([docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices)). GitHub's Spec Kit
(Sept 2025, labelled experimental) and AWS Kiro formalise this. Practitioner reviews are mixed:
specs help, but heavyweight SDD produces piles of markdown that humans don't really review. Agents
also still ignore parts of the spec, and the same spec gives different code on different runs
([Böckeler, Oct 2025](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/sdd-3-tools.html)).

**Takeaway:** use one short spec per feature (a page or less) with *executable* acceptance criteria.
Skip specs entirely for trivial changes. Don't adopt a whole SDD framework.

### 1.3 Test-driven guardrails and the reward-hacking problem

Tests are the strongest signal an agent has, so tests are also what agents learn to game.
ImpossibleBench found that test modification was Claude models' main cheating strategy. It also
found that hiding tests cuts cheating to near zero but hurts legitimate performance, and that a
clear "stop if the tests look wrong" instruction cuts cheating sharply
([arXiv:2510.20270](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20270); figures via
[LessWrong summary](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/qJYMbrabcQqCZ7iqm/impossiblebench-measuring-reward-hacking-in-llm-coding-1)).

**The practical design:**

- **Acceptance tests are written by a different agent, from the spec only**, before
  implementation. They must fail first ("red").
- **The tests are locked.** A Claude Code `PreToolUse` hook (exit code 2 blocks the call) refuses
  edits to `tests/acceptance/**` ([hooks docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks)). A CI step
  checks that those files match the hash recorded when the spec was approved.
- **The implementer can still see the tests**, since hiding them costs performance. It can also add
  its own unit tests.
- **The prompt contains an escape hatch.** If the implementer believes a locked test contradicts
  the spec, it stops and files a "spec conflict" instead of working around it.
- **Mutation testing on changed code** checks that the tests actually constrain behaviour. Meta's
  ACH work found that about half of its useful generated tests would have been thrown away under a
  coverage-only criterion ([arXiv:2501.12862](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12862)). Off-the-shelf
  tools: mutmut (Python), Stryker (JS/TS), cargo-mutants (Rust), PIT (Java).

### 1.4 Linters, formatters, type checks, CI gates

These are cheap, deterministic, and exactly what agents respond well to. The OpenAI harness post
stresses encoding architecture and "taste" as lints and structural tests rather than prose
([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/)). Two places to run them:

- **In the agent loop:** a `PostToolUse` hook auto-formats edited files, and a `Stop` hook runs the
  fast checks and refuses to let the agent finish while they fail
  ([hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks)).
- **In CI:** the same checks plus slower ones. Branch protection makes them required.

### 1.5 Multi-model and adversarial review

LLM judges prefer their own outputs ([e.g. arXiv:2601.06884](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.06884)).
The best direct study I found shows the picture is subtle
([Song, Oct 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01471)):

- A strong cross-model reviewer is roughly as good as the *same* model reviewing in a fresh session.
- The two catch different errors, with only ~41% overlap.
- One same-model review plus one cross-model review caught 56.7% of planted errors, versus 42.7%
  for two same-model reviews.
- A weak cross-model reviewer added nothing.

**Takeaway:** use two reviewers, both strong, both in fresh context, and preferably from different
vendors. Don't bother with a cheap third model as a "panel". Reuse what exists: Codex has native
GitHub PR review (`@codex review` or automatic), driven by your AGENTS.md
([OpenAI docs](https://developers.openai.com/codex/integrations/github)). Claude has an official
GitHub Action that can authenticate with a Pro/Max subscription token
([docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/github-actions)).

### 1.6 Sandboxing and permissions

- **Inside the agent:** Claude Code has OS-level sandboxing (bubblewrap on Linux) that restricts
  filesystem and network ([docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing)), and Codex has
  sandbox modes.
- **Outside the agent:** the stronger boundary is giving each task its own disposable VM. boat.dev
  provides exactly that: `new`/`fork` from snapshots, `stop`/`resume`, `run` (one-shot VM with a
  cost report), and per-sandbox usage.
- **Credentials:** OpenAI's CI guidance is a good pattern. The agent job runs with read-only repo
  permissions and emits a patch, and a separate job without the model key applies it
  ([Codex docs](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/non-interactive-mode)).
- **Supply chain:** LLMs hallucinate package names (5% for commercial models, ~22% for open models,
  and 43% of hallucinated names recur), which enables "slopsquatting"
  ([Kaspersky summary of Spracklen et al.](https://www.kaspersky.com/blog/ai-slopsquatting-supply-chain-risk/53327/)).
  New dependencies therefore need a gate.

### 1.7 Memory and context management

Context degrades as it grows ("context rot", [Chroma, Jul 2025](https://research.trychroma.com/context-rot)),
and big instruction files hurt ([arXiv:2602.11988](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988)). What works:

- A **short** `AGENTS.md`, now a Linux Foundation–stewarded standard read by Codex, Cursor, Copilot
  and others ([OpenAI/AAIF](https://openai.com/index/agentic-ai-foundation/)). Claude Code reads
  `CLAUDE.md`, which can import or point to it.
- **Docs as the system of record:** `docs/` holds architecture notes, decisions (ADRs) and specs.
  AGENTS.md is a *map* to them, not an encyclopedia
  ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/)).
- **Durable state in files, not chat history:** `tasks.json` (JSON, because models are less likely
  to rewrite it wholesale) and `progress.md`
  ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)).
- **Fresh sessions per task.** Subagents do exploration so the main context stays clean. Vector-DB
  "memory" is not needed at this scale; `grep` plus good docs wins.

### 1.8 Decomposition and parallel agents

Small tasks (one feature per session, diffs a reviewer can actually read) are the most reliable
pattern. Parallel agents help when tasks are truly independent. Each one gets its own sandbox or git
worktree, and they integrate through PRs. Parallelism multiplies cost, review load and merge
conflicts, so it belongs late in the build plan, not early.

### 1.9 Does any of this pay off? Be honest about the evidence

- METR's 2025 RCT found experienced open-source developers were **19% slower** with early-2025 AI
  tools, while believing they were faster.
- METR's Feb 2026 follow-up points to speedups (−18% and −4% time; all confidence intervals cross
  zero). METR says selection effects make the design unreliable
  ([METR](https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/)).

**Lesson for the harness:** measure it on your own tasks. Don't trust how fast it feels (§5).

## 2. Recommended architecture

### 2.1 Roles

| Role | Who | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Human (product owner)** | User | Approves spec and acceptance criteria; approves merge; answers escalations. About 10–20 min per feature. |
| **Planner / spec writer** | Claude Code (strongest Claude model, plan mode) | Strong at codebase exploration and planning; interactive with the user. |
| **Test author** | Codex (`codex exec`) | Different vendor from the implementer, so it doesn't share the implementer's blind spots. Writes acceptance tests from the spec alone. |
| **Implementer** | Claude Code headless (`claude -p`) in a boat sandbox | Best hooks system (PreToolUse/Stop gates), subagents, budgets. |
| **Fallback implementer** | Codex | Used when Claude limits are hit, or as a "second attempt" when Claude fails a task twice. |
| **Reviewer A** | Codex GitHub code review (automatic on PR) | Zero build effort; uses the subscription; reads AGENTS.md review rules. |
| **Reviewer B** | Fresh Claude session (`claude -p` with a review prompt and JSON schema) | Checks spec conformance and test integrity. Fresh context reduces self-preference. |
| **Tie-breaker / spec critic (optional)** | Grok (Grok Build headless, or chat) | Third opinion only when A and B disagree on a blocking issue, or as a critic of large specs. Kept off the critical path because quotas are unpublished. |
| **Gatekeeper** | GitHub Actions + branch protection (runners on GitHub or `runs-on: boat`) | Deterministic; no model can talk its way past it. |
| **Orchestrator** | `harness` CLI (Python, small), run from a long-lived "control" boat sandbox | Glue only: creates sandboxes, runs phases, enforces budgets, writes logs. |

     straight to implementation plus gates.
4. **Acceptance tests.** Codex writes executable tests from the spec only. The harness runs them and
   requires that they *fail*; a test that already passes isn't testing the new feature. The harness
   records their hashes in `.harness/locks.json` and commits them.
5. **Decompose.** Claude writes `tasks.json`: an ordered list of small tasks, each with a "done when"
   check, all `passes:false`.
6. **Implement.** The harness forks the golden snapshot into a task sandbox, clones the branch, and
   runs `claude -p` once per task with a fixed prompt. The prompt says: read AGENTS.md, progress.md
   and tasks.json; run `make smoke`; implement the next task; run `make check`; commit; update
   progress.
   - **Hooks enforce the rules:** format on edit, block edits to locked paths and lint config, and a
     Stop gate that runs `make check` with at most N forced continuations.
   - **Budgets:** `--max-budget-usd` (or turn caps under a subscription) and a wall-clock timeout.
   - If a task fails twice, the harness retries once with Codex as implementer. If that fails too,
     it escalates.
7. **PR.** The harness pushes the branch and opens a PR whose body is generated from the spec
   checklist, gate results, a diff summary, screenshots or e2e output, cost and time.
8. **Gates.** GitHub Actions runs the required checks (§3). Failures are fed back to the
   implementer automatically.
9. **Review.**
   - Codex auto-review and the Claude fresh review run in parallel. Claude's review prompt
     focuses on spec conformance, test integrity (were tests weakened, skipped or special-cased?),
     security, and fit with the existing architecture.
   - Findings are structured JSON. *Blocking* findings go back to the implementer; at most two
     rounds, then the user decides.
   - Reviewer disagreements go to Grok or the user.
10. **Human checkpoint 2.** The user reads the PR summary (not necessarily the diff), tries the
    preview URL if it's a web app (`host <port>` from the sandbox), and merges. Branch protection
    guarantees the gates passed.
11. **Ratchet.** After merge, the harness asks: *did review or the user catch something a gate
    could catch next time?* If so, it proposes a lint rule, test or one-line AGENTS.md addition as a
    tiny follow-up PR. This is how quality compounds without the instruction file growing.

---

## 3. Components

**R** = reuse an existing tool, **C** = configure an existing tool, **B** = build (by AI).

| # | Component | Purpose | Reuse / build |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Golden sandbox snapshot** | Reproducible environment with Claude Code, Codex CLI, gh, language toolchain, Playwright | C: boat.dev `snapshot`/`fork`; a `bootstrap.sh` (B, tiny) |
| 2 | **Project template repo** | The quality floor every project starts from | B: assembled from standard tools |
| 3 | Formatter + linter | Style and bug-pattern enforcement | R: Ruff (Py) / Biome or ESLint+Prettier (TS) |
| 4 | Type checker | Catches interface errors early | R: mypy or pyright / `tsc --strict` |
| 5 | Test runner + property tests | Unit and acceptance tests | R: pytest + Hypothesis / Vitest + fast-check |
| 6 | E2E / browser checks | "Test like a user" | R: Playwright (+ Playwright MCP for agents) |
| 7 | Mutation testing (diff-scoped) | Are the tests meaningful? | R: mutmut / Stryker (incremental mode) |
| 8 | Diff coverage | Changed lines are tested | R: diff-cover / Vitest coverage + script |
| 9 | Secret scanning | No keys in commits | R: gitleaks (pre-commit + CI) |
| 10 | SAST | Common vulnerability patterns | R: Semgrep (community rules) |
| 11 | Dependency gate | Block hallucinated or vulnerable packages | R: osv-scanner + Dependabot/Renovate; B: tiny "new deps need approval" check |
| 12 | `make check` / `make smoke` | One command for agents, hooks and CI alike | B (trivial) |
| 13 | pre-commit hooks | Local fast checks | R: pre-commit framework |
| 14 | CI workflow + branch protection | The merge gate | C: GitHub Actions; optional `runs-on: boat` |
| 15 | **AGENTS.md + CLAUDE.md** | Short map: commands, layout, rules, where docs live | B: < 100 lines, human-approved |
| 16 | **Claude Code hooks + settings** | Format-on-edit, locked-path guard, Stop gate, permission allowlist, sandbox on | C: `.claude/settings.json` + small scripts (B) |
| 17 | Codex config | Same rules for Codex; review guidelines | C: AGENTS.md + `config.toml` |
| 18 | **Spec, task and progress templates** | `docs/specs/TEMPLATE.md`, `tasks.json` schema, `progress.md` | B |
| 19 | **Test lock** | Hash file + CI check + hook | B (~50 lines) |
| 20 | **Reviewer B** | Fresh Claude review → JSON → PR comment + status check | B: prompt + JSON schema + script; or C: `anthropics/claude-code-action` |
| 21 | Reviewer A | Independent review | C: Codex GitHub code review toggle |
| 22 | **Orchestrator `harness`** | Runs the pipeline, budgets, logs, escalation | B: Python CLI calling `boat`, `gh`, `claude -p`, `codex exec` |
| 23 | **Run log + report** | Per-run JSONL (phase, cost, time, gate results); weekly markdown report | B |
| 24 | **Eval suite** | Private benchmark of the harness itself | B: 15–30 tasks in a sample repo with hidden tests |
| 25 | Notifications | Tell the user when a spec or PR needs them | R: GitHub notifications (default); optional boat webhook |

The pieces to build are #2, 12, 15, 16, 18, 19, 20, 22, 23 and 24. The target is **under ~2,000
lines of harness code** in total. Everything else is configuration of mainstream tools the user can
Google.

**What I deliberately leave out:**

- Vector-DB memory.
- Agent frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, …).
- Custom web dashboards.
- Kubernetes.
- Self-hosted model gateways.
- Swarms of role-play agents.

None of these address a failure mode found in the research, and each one adds something the user
would have to maintain.

---

## 4. Phased build plan (AI builds everything)

**Conventions for every phase:**

- One phase equals roughly one sitting (1–4 hours of agent time).
- Each phase has a deliverable and an **objective done check** that a script can run.
- The done check is written *first*, in the phase's opening commit, so the phase can't redefine
  "done" at the end.
- Claude Code is the builder. Codex reviews each phase's PR.

**Bootstrapping:**

- Phases 0–3 are built interactively by Claude Code with the user, because the gates don't exist
  yet.
- Once phase 3 lands, **every later phase is delivered as PRs that must pass phases 1–3's gates and
  reviews**.
- Once phase 5 lands, later phases are run *by* `harness run` itself. The harness lives in its own
  repo (`harness/`), which uses the template from phase 1, so it is gated like any other project.

### Phase 0 — Decisions and golden sandbox
- **Deliverable:** answers to §7's open questions in `DECISIONS.md`; a boat sandbox with Claude Code,
  Codex CLI, gh, the chosen toolchain and Playwright, saved as a named snapshot; `bootstrap.sh` to
  recreate it.
- **Done check:** `boat run` on a fresh fork executes `scripts/doctor.sh`, which prints every tool's
  version and runs a one-line headless prompt to *both* `claude -p` and `codex exec`. Exit code 0.

### Phase 1 — Template repo with the quality floor
- **Deliverable:** `template-<lang>` repo with formatter, linter, type checker, test runner,
  pre-commit, gitleaks, Semgrep, `make check`, a CI workflow and branch protection on `main`.
- **Done check:** a script opens six throwaway PRs. Five each contain exactly one defect (format
  error, lint error, type error, failing test, fake secret) and must each be **blocked** by the
  right check. The sixth is clean and must pass.

### Phase 2 — Agent guardrails
- **Deliverable:** AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md (short); `.claude/settings.json` with permission
  allowlist, sandboxing on, and hooks (format-on-edit, locked-path guard, Stop gate running
  `make check` with a retry cap); matching Codex config.
- **Done check:** `tests/harness/test_hooks.sh` runs headless Claude in a sandbox with three
  adversarial prompts and asserts:
  - "edit tests/acceptance/x.py to make it pass" is blocked;
  - "stop now", with a failing test, gets a forced continuation;
  - a request to `curl` an unapproved host is denied.

### Phase 3 — Review bot
- **Deliverable:**
  - Codex auto-review enabled.
  - Reviewer B workflow, with a prompt and JSON schema `{blocking:[…], nits:[…], test_integrity:…}`,
    posting a PR comment and a status check.
  - A **seeded-bug PR set**: 10 PRs, each with one known defect (off-by-one, injection, missing auth
    check, swallowed exception, weakened assertion, skipped test, …), plus 5 clean PRs.
- **Done check:** the combined reviewers flag at least 8 of the 10 defects as blocking, and
  false-block at most 1 of the 5 clean PRs. Results are saved as the review baseline.

**→ From here on, all harness work arrives as gated, reviewed PRs.**

### Phase 4 — Spec and locked acceptance tests
- **Deliverable:** spec template; `harness spec` (Claude writes the spec, Codex critiques it);
  `harness tests` (Codex writes tests, the harness checks they fail, records hashes); a CI
  lock-check job.
- **Done check:**
  - A PR that modifies a locked test fails CI.
  - An **impossible-task canary**: a spec whose locked test contradicts it. The implementer must
    emit a "spec conflict" and not produce a passing build. Run it 3 times; 0 cheats allowed.

### Phase 5 — Orchestrator end-to-end
- **Deliverable:** `harness run <issue>`. It forks the sandbox, runs spec → (approval) → tests → plan
  → implement → PR, enforces budgets (turns, dollars, wall clock) and escalation, and writes a
  JSONL run log.
- **Done check:** 3 real small features in a sample app reach a merged PR with the human doing
  only "approve spec" and "merge". Each has a run log with cost and time. A forced-runaway test (a
  task that can't be finished) stops at its budget and escalates.

### Phase 6 — Eval suite and metrics
- **Deliverable:**
  - `evals/` with 15–30 tasks (bug fixes, small features, refactors) in a sample repo, each with
    **hidden tests** that agents never see.
  - `harness eval`, which runs the suite in parallel sandboxes and writes a scorecard.
  - A CI rule: harness PRs must include a before/after eval delta.
- **Done check:** a baseline scorecard is committed. Re-running the suite gives a pass rate within
  ±10 points of the baseline, which shows the noise level is known.

### Phase 7 — Deeper verification
- **Deliverable:** diff-scoped mutation testing gate; diff-coverage gate; Playwright e2e smoke with
  screenshots in the PR; dependency allowlist gate.
- **Done check:** a seeded PR with tests that execute but assert nothing passes coverage but
  **fails** the mutation gate. A PR adding a non-existent package fails the dependency gate.

### Phase 8 — Parallelism (only if needed)
- **Deliverable:** `harness run --parallel`. Independent tasks go to separate sandboxes, each opens
  its own PR, and the harness serialises merges and rebases.
- **Done check:** two independent features run concurrently, both merge green, and total cost is
  no more than 2.3× a single run.

### Phase 9 — Ratchet and upkeep
- **Deliverable:**
  - A post-merge retro step that proposes lint rules or tests from review findings.
  - Renovate/Dependabot.
  - A weekly report (eval trend, cost, escaped bugs).
  - `harness doctor`, which checks that tools, auth and the snapshot are healthy.
- **Done check:** a seeded recurring review finding produces an auto-proposed lint or test PR. The
  weekly report is generated by a scheduled job.

**Each phase is a stopping point that is still useful on its own.** After phase 3 the user already
has a much safer workflow, even without the orchestrator.

---

## 5. Quality bar: how we know it works

**By construction (must be 100%):** every merged PR passed all required checks, has a spec (or a
`small` label), has locked acceptance tests that were red before and green after, and has two
reviews with no unresolved blocking findings. Branch protection enforces this.

**Measured (targets are starting points; reset them after the phase 6 baseline):**

| Metric | How measured | Starting target |
|---|---|---|
| Hidden-test pass rate on eval suite | `harness eval` | Baseline, then no harness PR may drop it by >5 points |
| First-pass yield | % of runs that reach a mergeable PR with no human code edits | ≥ 70% for small features |
| Escaped defects | Bugs labelled `escaped` linked to a merged PR | < 1 per 5 features, trending down |
| Mutation score on changed code | mutmut/Stryker diff mode | ≥ 60% at first, ratchet to 75% |
| Diff coverage | diff-cover | ≥ 80% |
| Reviewer recall / false-block rate | Seeded-bug PR set, re-run monthly and after model changes | ≥ 80% / ≤ 20% |
| Test-tampering canary | Impossible-task canaries in the eval suite | **0** tolerated |
| Human minutes per feature | Self-reported in the merge comment (one number) | Trending down; tells us if the user is just rubber-stamping |
| Cost and time per merged feature | Run log | Within the agreed budget (§7) |
| Code health trend | Complexity and duplication (Ruff/ESLint rules, jscpd) per month | Not getting worse |

**Rule for harness changes** (new prompt, new model, new hook): accept only if the eval pass rate is
not worse, the canary stays at 0, and cost doesn't rise more than ~20% without a matching quality
gain. This keeps the harness honest as models change.

---

## 6. Risks and failure modes

| Risk | How it shows up | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **Reward hacking** | Agent edits or weakens tests, special-cases inputs, adds `skip`, swallows errors | Split authorship; locked acceptance tests (hook + CI hash); hidden eval tests; mutation testing; reviewer checks test integrity; "stop and report a spec conflict" escape hatch; impossible-task canaries |
| **Runaway agents and cost** | Infinite fix loops, huge diffs, long sandbox lifetimes | `--max-budget-usd` / turn caps, wall-clock timeouts, Stop-hook retry cap, max 2 review rounds, sandbox TTL and auto-stop, `boat limits` checked before fan-out, per-feature budget in `harness.toml`, a kill switch (`harness stop`, which interrupts and stops all sandboxes) |
| **Subscription rate limits** | Claude's 5-hour and weekly caps, a separate Opus cap ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2025/07/28/anthropic-unveils-new-rate-limits-to-curb-claude-code-power-users/)); Codex review quotas ([pricing](https://developers.openai.com/codex/pricing)); unpublished Grok quotas | Role fallback (Codex implements if Claude is capped, and vice versa); a cheaper model for routine tasks and the top model for planning and review; the queue pauses rather than failing; no parallelism until phase 8; check `/usage` and `boat limits` |
| **Terms of service** | Subscription tokens used in unattended CI may be treated differently from interactive use ([open question on Claude setup-tokens in CI](https://claudeissues.com/issue/27125-question-oauth-setup-token-policy-for-scheduled-ci-cd-automation-github-actions)) | Run agents inside the user's own boat sandboxes, where the user logged in. Keep CI deterministic (no model calls required). Use the vendors' first-party integrations (Codex GitHub review, claude-code-action). If heavy automation is wanted, budget a small pay-as-you-go API key. |
| **Security: secrets** | Keys leak into repos or logs, or get exfiltrated by a prompt-injected agent | No production credentials in task sandboxes; secrets via boat env settings, never files; gitleaks; Claude sandbox network restrictions; agent jobs get read-only tokens where possible |
| **Security: prompt injection** | Malicious text in issues, dependency READMEs or web pages steers the agent | Only the user's own issues trigger runs; network allowlist; review gate; no auto-merge |
| **Security: supply chain** | Hallucinated or typosquatted packages | Dependency allowlist gate; osv-scanner; lockfiles; human approval of new deps (listed in the PR summary) |
| **Spec drift / wrong feature** | Correct code for the wrong thing | Human spec checkpoint; acceptance tests derived from the spec; preview URL before merge |
| **Review fatigue / rubber-stamping** | User merges without reading | One-page PR summaries; risk labels (`small`, `normal`, `risky`); track human minutes; never auto-merge `risky` |
| **Quality erosion over time** | Duplication, bloated files, architecture decay that individual PRs don't reveal | Structural lints; complexity and duplication trend in the weekly report; a periodic "cleanup" run (OpenAI's team needed this "garbage collection") |
| **Lock-in** | Harness tied to one vendor's features | AGENTS.md (open standard), plain git + GitHub Actions + Make, model roles in one config file; Claude-specific hooks are small scripts that could be ported to Codex rules |
| **Complexity the user won't maintain** | The harness becomes its own project nobody understands | <2k lines of custom code; boring tools; each phase useful on its own; `harness doctor`; a plain-English `HOW_IT_WORKS.md`; harness changes go through evals, so the user doesn't have to judge them |
| **Flaky gates** | E2E or mutation tests fail randomly, so people learn to ignore red | Mark and quarantine flaky tests; retry once in CI; diff-scope the slow gates; the weekly report lists flaky checks |
| **Model churn** | A new model behaves differently; prompts rot | Eval suite + seeded-bug set re-run on every model or prompt change; roles configurable |
| **Over-process** | Every typo needs a spec | `small` fast lane: gates only. Specs only for new behaviour. |

---

## 7. Open questions for the user

1. **What will you build with it?** Web apps, CLIs/scripts, APIs, mobile? This picks the default
   language and template. My suggestion is **Python** or **TypeScript**, not both, to start.
2. **New projects, existing repos, or both?** Existing repos need an "adopt" step (add the template
   gates and baseline the current failures) and more conservative autonomy.
3. **Monthly budget ceiling** for boat.dev credits plus any pay-as-you-go API usage, and a
   per-feature cap. Are you willing to upgrade a plan tier if limits bite?
4. **Autonomy level:** always merge yourself (recommended), or allow auto-merge for `small` changes
   once the metrics are good?
5. **Where do you want to interact?** GitHub issues and PRs (recommended), the CLI in a boat
   sandbox, or chat (e.g. through the Grok "Model Council" bot)? How should you be notified?
6. **Grok's role:** spec critic and tie-breaker (my suggestion), a full third reviewer, or a backup
   implementer? Depends on how much Grok Build quota you actually get.
7. **Public or private repos?** This affects Codex/Claude GitHub app access, Actions minutes, and
   whether boat CI runners are worth using.
8. **How much time per feature** are you willing to spend reading specs and PR summaries? This sets
   spec length and how much detail summaries need.
9. **Any hard constraints:** data that must never leave your machine, licences to avoid, deploy
   targets (Vercel, Fly, a VPS?), and whether deployment is in scope at all.
10. **Comfort with API keys:** subscriptions only (cheaper, rate-limited, ToS grey areas in CI), or a
    small pay-as-you-go key for CI-side automation?

---

## Sources

Primary unless marked. All accessed 2026-11-17.
